title: Addas and the grapes
hook: a Christian servant from Nineveh brings him grapes and hears him speak of Yunus (sirah)

segments.voice: Yesterday, du'a. Your line was: if you're not angry, I don't mind. When something went badly, whose opinion turned out to matter to you? Day seven hundred fifty-two.
screen: `IF YOU'RE NOT ANGRY, I DON'T MIND.`

segments.voice: Two brothers own the orchard where he's resting, Utba and Shayba, sons of Rabi'a, men of Quraysh who are no friends of his message. They've watched what Ta'if did to him. And something in them moves. Ibn Ishaq says they felt for him as a kinsman. They call their servant, a Christian man named Addas, and tell him: take a bunch of these grapes on a plate, and bring it to that man, and tell him to eat. Today: Addas.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS WATCH.` → `A PLATE OF GRAPES.` → `CARRIED BY ADDAS.`

segments.voice: Addas sets the grapes down. The Prophet reaches out, and before he eats, he says, in the name of Allah. Addas looks at him. These are not words, he says, that the people of this country say. So the Prophet asks him: where are you from, Addas, and what is your religion? Addas says he is a Christian, from Nineveh. And the Prophet answers: from the town of the righteous man Yunus, son of Matta. Now Addas is astonished. How do you know who Yunus son of Matta was? In Ibn Ishaq's account the Prophet says: he is my brother. He was a prophet, and I am a prophet. And Addas bends over him and kisses his head, and his hands, and his feet. Over by the wall, one brother says to the other: well, he's spoiled your servant for you. When Addas comes back they scold him, and he answers that there is nothing on earth better than this man; he told me something only a prophet would know. Look at who meets here. A man who has just been driven out by his own kind. A servant far from home, in a town where nobody says what he says. And between them, a name both of them know: Yunus, whom the Qur'an remembers as one of the messengers, the man of the fish. Christians and Jews tell his story too, as Jonah. What opens the door is not an argument. It's a plate of grapes, two words said before eating, and a question about where someone comes from. And notice who sent the grapes: two men who did not share his faith.
screen: `IN THE NAME OF ALLAH.` · `WHERE ARE YOU FROM, ADDAS?` · `NINEVEH: THE TOWN OF YUNUS.` · `HE IS MY BROTHER.` · then, large: `A BOWL OF GRAPES.`

segments.voice: The practice: offer food to someone who's tired. For now, sit, and breathe. Think through your day and your week for one person who is running on empty. A coworker on a double shift. A parent with a newborn. A friend who just got bad news. Someone far from home. Picture what you could bring them: a piece of fruit, a sandwich, a cup of tea, a meal dropped at the door. Keep it small and real. Then picture one question you could ask them, like the Prophet asked Addas: where are you from? how are you holding up? If you pray, you can say bismillah before you eat today. The bell holds the time.
Addas. A Christian servant from Nineveh who carries grapes to a rejected man, hears him say Allah's name and speak of Yunus, and kisses his hands. Today's word.
Your line: a bowl of grapes. Today, bring something to eat to one tired person, and ask them one real question while you're there. Day seven hundred fifty-two.

screen: `DAY 752 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE ANGEL OF THE MOUNTAINS.`

howItsDone: Muslims retell the meeting with Addas as part of the Ta'if story, and say bismillah, in the name of Allah, before eating.

fork.setup: you're Addas. a stranger says Allah's name over the grapes you brought, and then names your hometown's prophet. what do you do?
options: leave the plate and go back.
ask how he knows of Yunus.
fork.reveal: Addas asked how he knew; when he heard 'he is my brother, a prophet', he kissed his head, hands and feet.

original.note: Arabic: grapes; the fruit Addas carried on the plate.

trapdoor: what you thought: someone gave him a snack.
what it means: in his lowest hour, kindness came from people outside his faith, and a stranger recognized him.
what a scholar hears: Ibn Ishaq's account; Yunus son of Matta of Nineveh, whom the Qur'an names among the messengers (37:139).

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (Utba and Shayba send Addas with grapes; bismillah; Nineveh; 'he is my brother, he was a prophet and I am a prophet'; Addas kisses his head, hands and feet)

notes: All dialogue is paraphrased from Ibn Ishaq as recalled; confirm, especially 'he told me something only a prophet would know'.
Index hook said Addas 'recognizes him in the name of Yunus'; the hook here was rephrased to follow the sirah's order (bismillah, then Nineveh, then Yunus). Confirm.
Qur'an 37:139 is paraphrased; Pickthall wording not quoted.
The brief mention that Christians and Jews tell Jonah's story is a neighbor note, not a comparison; confirm.
Practice invites saying bismillah 'if you pray'; confirm that framing.
Editor pass: the Qur'an does not name Nineveh; moved the Nineveh link to the sirah in the teach and myth.
